display.title: Ki B'Simcha Teitzei'u: The Tzemach Tzedek's Three Words
display.summary_short: The Rebbe's Purim lesson on the three pesukim said after davening, and a Chassid who saves his business by singing with simcha, as the Tzemach Tzedek advised.
display.summary_long: The storyteller begins with the Midrash: the Torah learning of Jewish children helped overturn Haman's decree, and Mordechai, seeking a sign from Heaven, asked three children for the pasuk they had just learned. Each answered with an encouraging verse, the same three pesukim we say at the end of davening. He then explains a sichah the Rebbe gave to children before Purim: every action has three stages, thought, speech and deed, and so did Haman's plot; today the yetzer hara follows the same steps, bringing darkness, telling a child he is too tired to daven or make a brachah, and pulling him away from shul on Shabbos morning, and each pasuk answers one stage. The story follows a wealthy Chassid of the Tzemach Tzedek who sells seed grain to the poritzim and must deliver on the exact day. Halfway to the inn he realizes he left the richest poritz's wagon at home. Instead of despairing, he forces himself to sing a happy niggun and treats the poritzim to drinks. That night a downpour ruins all the grain, and the poritzim pay him in full anyway. He explains that the Tzemach Tzedek had told him three words: ki b'simcha teitzei'u, with joy you will go out.
display.lesson: Simcha brings a person out of his troubles; even when you do not feel happy, act joyful and the joy will follow. The yetzer hara's plans will not succeed, because Hashem is with us.

advisories.note: The Chassid serves the poritzim a strong punch and they fall asleep drunk; told humorously.
